Chip stocks had a rough week, and the trouble didn't start at a chipmaker. A spike in the bond yields of CoreWeave, a cloud provider that rents out AI computing power, revived worries about debt-heavy AI customers and dragged semiconductor shares lower, according to Yahoo Finance. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), both an investor in CoreWeave and its chip supplier, slipped with the group.

Nvidia designs the processors and networking gear that train and run AI models, and sells them as complete data center systems to cloud giants, AI labs, and specialists like CoreWeave. Gamers know it for its graphics cards, but data centers now bring in the vast majority of its revenue.

So the selloff raised a sharp question: is Nvidia's growth only as sturdy as the balance sheets of the companies buying its chips? The answer depends less on one cloud provider than on who else is paying.

A Supplier With Software-Like Margins

Whatever its customers are doing, Nvidia itself is enormously profitable. Over the past 12 months, it earned $192.88 billion in net income and kept about 65% of its sales as operating profit. Those margins come from pricing power: buyers pay up because Nvidia sells the chips, the networking, and the software developers already build on.

That edge has compounded for years, with revenue growing about 66.9% a year over the past five years. AI spending has been the common thread for the wider chip group covered in 12 Best Performing Semiconductor Stocks to Invest In.

NVIDIA’s Strategic Partnership With Synopsys Aims to Accelerate AI-First R&D
Demand Is Coming From More Directions

The latest results show the moat widening. In its fiscal second quarter of 2027, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and data center revenue rose 117% to $89.0 billion. Management guided third-quarter revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, without counting on any data center compute sales in China.

The customer list argues against a single point of failure. The new Vera Rubin platform is in full production at partners including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle, not just CoreWeave, and CEO Jensen Huang said in the release that a broader base of AI labs and startups is scaling at the same time. Nvidia is also lining up outside money: financing platforms with firms including Apollo, BlackRock, and KKR aim to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital, subject to final agreements. The buildout behind those orders runs well beyond chips, into the names in 15 Best Data Center Stocks to Buy and Hold for the Next Decade.

The last few years have been absolutely fantastic for stock investors. The bull market of the last four years has pushed the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) 116% higher while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) is up an even more impressive 156%.

While the bull market has been strong and supported by stellar earnings growth and improving outlooks, many investors can't help but notice that stock market valuations are particularly high. That's not a sustainable position for stocks: Either earnings have to grow fast enough to bring valuations lower, or stock prices have to come down.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In fact, it's a practical inevitability that stock prices crash 20% or more in the future. The markets move in cycles, and eventually, some event will trigger a big sell-off in the stock market. If you want to position your portfolio to recover in less than half the time it takes for others, here's exactly what you should do.

Image source: Getty Images.
The best portfolio for a market crash

It doesn't take any groundbreaking portfolio strategy to produce rapid recoveries in the event of a stock market crash. Investors can hold a simple 60/40 stock/bond portfolio with periodic rebalancing and achieve superior results in maintaining portfolio stability.

Since 1988, the 60/40 portfolio has recovered from drawdowns of 20% or more in just 11 months on average, according to data compiled by J.P. Morgan analysts. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 took an average of 24 months to recover, even with dividends reinvested.

It's worth noting that the 60/40 portfolio only stands out against an all-stock portfolio in terms of recovery when the portfolio drops at least 20%. Smaller drops don't exhibit much difference in how long it takes the portfolio to recover. That said, that's exactly the kind of protection an investor should hope for from bonds: a stabilizing force amid big long drops without providing too much drag amid shorter pullbacks.

The stability of the 60/40 portfolio is further evidenced by the likelihood that it will produce a positive return over any given five- or 10-year period. Since 1989, the 60/40 portfolio has produced a positive return 99% of the time over any five-year period and 100% of the time over 10 years. The S&P 500 alone only achieves positive returns 87% of the time over five years and 93% of the time over 10 years.

One great quarter doesn't justify going overboard on Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) purchases, though owning some is a great idea, and adding a little right now still makes a lot of sense given what could be on the way. The coin surged by 66% in the third quarter, marking its best quarter since its wild run in 2021, while the S&P 500 gained just 2% amid considerable global uncertainty.

Bullish investors are already sounding off in anticipation of the uptrend continuing. Tom Lee, chairman of BitMine Immersion Technologies, says Ethereum is "dwarfing" other major assets. At least for Q3, he's right. Let's take a closer look at the case for loading up and discuss why it's best to keep overly bullish inclinations in check for the time being.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
It's still down 37% over five years

One compelling reason not to bet the farm on Ethereum is that it still trades below its level five years ago.

Ether is down by 37% over the last five years. An index fund tracking the S&P 500 would have returned 85% with dividends reinvested. Even with the index frozen in place, Ether would need to gain quite a lot to catch up, and that might take a while, if it happens.

That's a tall order, but it's not an entirely absurd proposition for an asset that just gained 66% in a quarter. Pulling off a recovery to surpass the market's benchmark return would vindicate everyone who held through the slump and go a long way toward repairing the coin's reputation.

But investors should know that a climbing chart is not the same as having an investment thesis. Getting too enthusiastic with purchasing at the moment could quickly become a poor decision if Ethereum cools down a bit.

It's still worth buying

Ethereum is worth owning because it's the main hub for capital in the crypto universe.

Today, Ethereum hosts $147.9 billion in stablecoins and $17 billion in tradeable tokenized real-world assets. This means it has billions in assets, such as Treasury bills, recorded as crypto tokens on its blockchain. Capital tends to accumulate where there's already capital, and especially where there's an avenue to convert stored capital into a yield or a return. Ethereum's decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem offers both of those features more than any other crypto network.

David Tepper is one of the most successful hedge fund investors in the world. His Appaloosa Limited Partnership compounded at roughly 25% annualized after fees from its founding in 1993 through 2019, when he began returning cash to outside investors.

Today, roughly 90% of the capital in Appaloosa belongs to Tepper himself, and he continues to produce phenomenal returns. Through the first half of the year, the fund was up 32%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

While Tepper has kept a significant amount of cash on hand, concentrated bets on a handful of stocks have helped drive those returns. Around 40% of his public equity portfolio is held in just three stocks, according to the fund's most recent 13-F filing. Here's whether they're still worth buying today.

David Tepper, Appaloosa Management founder. Image source: Getty Images.
1. Amazon (17.7% of equities)

Tepper doubled his stake in Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) in the first quarter and added to it in the second quarter, making it the largest holding in his portfolio. His 5 million shares are worth about $1.25 billion as of this writing.

Amazon is both the world's largest online retailer and cloud computing platform. Amazon has successfully built a wide moat around its e-commerce business by developing a massive logistics network. Over the last few years, management has focused on improving efficiencies to drive operating margin higher.

At the same time, it's spending huge sums of cash to add compute capacity for its cloud computing business, Amazon Web Services (AWS). That's pushed its free cash flow into negative territory over the last 12 months. CEO Andy Jassy argues that Amazon has a clear view toward strong returns on the invested capital, thanks to long-term contracts with its customers and relatively short payback periods on new servers and networking equipment.

This isn't Amazon's first major investment cycle that's pushed free cash flow into negative territory. Amazon has executed this playbook in the past, and it's ultimately grown to produce much more free cash flow over the long run. While the stock is trading above its March and April lows, shares still look attractive at 30 times forward earnings expectations.

2. Micron Technology (12.4%)

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) is one of the three main memory chipmakers in the world. Tepper also has exposure to its Korean competitors through an ETF. Micron stock climbed more than 300% through the first half of 2026, prompting Tepper to cut his stake in the company by about 41% last quarter. Even so, it remains one of his top holdings.

Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) went public through a direct listing six years ago. It started trading at $10 per share, but it's now worth about $186 per share. Let's see why this tech stock delivered such massive gains -- and if it's still worth buying today in this choppy market.

Why did Palantir's stock soar?

Palantir operates two data-aggregating platforms: Gotham for government clients and Foundry for commercial clients. Both of these platforms create "digital twins" of a client's entire organization by gathering information through databases, supply chain reports, sensors, emails, internal documents, financial records, and even social media accounts.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Palantir uses its Ontology data model to unify that fragmented data into an easy-to-query stream of information for non-technical users. Its clients can access that data to make better data-driven decisions, and it connects leading large language models (including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude) to its platform via its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP).

Palantir's silo-busting tools are becoming essential as the AI race drives more government organizations and companies to upgrade their data mining capabilities. That's why many U.S. government agencies already use Gotham to plan their projects and missions, and why large companies like Walmart use Foundry to streamline their businesses.

Unlike many other high-growth tech companies, Palantir turned firmly profitable in 2023. It was added to the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) and the Nasdaq-100 in 2024.

From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect Palantir's revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 59% and 70%, respectively, as the AI market expands. Its stock isn't cheap at 87 times next year's earnings, but its explosive growth rates could justify that premium valuation.

Is Palantir's stock worth buying today?

Palantir expects global conflicts to fuel Gotham's growth through new government contracts, and the AI race to drive the expansion of its U.S. commercial business.

However, rising interest rates and Treasury yields could compress its valuation as more investors sell their higher-growth stocks to buy more conservative investments. Palantir's controversial reputation (due to its integration into immigration enforcement, mass surveillance, and military combat software) could also weigh down its stock.

Nvidia Doubled Revenue and Guided a Year Out

On September 28, Nvidia added $150 billion to its buyback, lifting the total authorization to $235 billion through fiscal 2028. That total is 9.0 times the record $26 billion Nvidia returned to shareholders in Q2. By early October, Nvidia stock had reached its high for the year.

Quantum computing is developing quicker than most investors realize. For a long time, 2030 was the year that most quantum computing firms pointed to as the arrival date of commercially viable quantum computing. That timeline has accelerated to 2029 as the technology has progressed, potentially making a new computing paradigm right around the corner.

Investors want to profit from this any way they can, and one of the most obvious ways is to pick a pure play like IonQ (NYSE: IONQ). IonQ is my top quantum computing investment, and it looks primed to be an incredible performer over the next five years.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ is casting a wide net

IonQ is tackling all sectors of quantum computing. The first and most obvious entry way is to develop a viable quantum computer that provides valuable insights in a different manner than traditional computing. It's getting closer to delivering its 256-qubit system and expects these units to start selling in early 2027. There are already preorders for some of these units, and if they are successful, it could see wider early-stage adoption.

This will lay the groundwork for more impressive computers, but it's a great start for now.

Another area where IonQ is looking to integrate vertically is through chip production. IonQ closed its acquisition of SkyWater, which gives it access to a chip fabrication firm. This allows IonQ to design and manufacture its quantum chips in-house, giving it an advantage over others in its industry.

Another major part of the quantum computing investment thesis is cybersecurity. Quantum computers will be able to break current encryption incredibly fast and render current state-of-the-art security methods useless. This is a big problem, but could also be a major opportunity.

IonQ will be playing both sides of this game, selling computers while also selling cybersecurity products to defend against these new capabilities. It took steps this week to secure that future by purchasing Elisity, a cybersecurity provider, for $1.3 billion.

All these moves are positioning IonQ as a major player in the quantum computing industry. IonQ will be able to make components, the computers themselves, provide software to utilize the devices, and protect against some of the threats they could pose. That's a highly vertically integrated company, and we could be witnessing the birth of a big tech superpower for the quantum age.

Adanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) investors have enjoyed some incredible gains during 2026. Currently, AMD is the ninth-best-performing component of the S&P 500, returning about 160% so far this year. While that figure was closer to 200% before the most recent sell-off, I think this is a wake-up call for most investors.

The reality is that AMD's stock got way too ahead of itself, and its valuation far outpaces its growth expectations. That is a major red flag for investors, and there are a few items investors need to keep an eye on as to when AMD could be a good buy again (hint: It won't be for a while).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD is gaining ground, but not fast enough

The entire AMD investment thesis circles around AMD catching up to Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and taking market share. On the surface, it appears that AMD is making headway. It has huge projects like OpenAI's computing cluster, which is starting to be delivered, and is powering Meta Muse from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). This has all led to stronger growth for AMD, with its data center division reporting $6.7 billion in revenue and growing by 107%. Overall, this helped the company grow its revenue 50% year over year to $11.5 billion in Q2.

Those are strong results that should be celebrated, but the problem is, it just isn't enough to catch Nvidia. During Q2, Nvidia's data center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% year over year. Overall revenue rose to $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. While AMD appears on the surface to be doing better, the reality is that Nvidia's lead is widening.

What makes matters worse is that Nvidia's Q2 results don't include any revenue from its upcoming generation of Vera Rubin architecture chips. This new generation promises major improvements, and they also cost more than previous generations. This will further exaggerate Nvidia's lead over AMD and eliminate the thesis that AMD is catching up.

But don't tell AMD's stock that, because according to it, AMD has won the AI arms race.

AMD's stock has uncoupled from its business

Over the long term, stocks and business growth are highly correlated. Over the short term, any number of factors can influence a stock's price. This is why long-term investing is easier for individual investors, as we can afford to wait for the business results to influence the stock price as long as we've found a company with a great long-term growth thesis.

As interest rates and Treasury yields rise, more investors will likely sell their stocks to buy CDs, T-bills, and other low-risk fixed-income investments. That shift could cause many tech stocks, which were lifted higher by AI tailwinds over the past few years, to pull back sharply.

If that tech sell-off happens, investors should consider buying an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that tracks all of the top tech stocks rather than betting on a single stock's recovery. One of those top ETFs is the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), which passively tracks the Nasdaq-100. Let's see why it's still a compelling ETF to buy if the market pulls back this year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What does QQQ track?

The Nasdaq-100 comprises the 100 largest non-financial stocks in the Nasdaq Composite Index (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC). It intentionally excludes financial stocks, which account for roughly 3% of the index, because they're more dependent on interest rate cycles than on innovative new products or organic growth. The index is rebalanced quarterly and reconstituted annually, so it constantly prunes the weaker companies while adding higher-growth ones.

QQQ's top holdings currently include Nvidia (8.1% of its portfolio), Apple (7.7%), Microsoft (6.2%), Micron (4.5%), and AMD (4.2%). Those are also the S&P 500's (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) biggest non-financial stocks, but QQQ allocates larger slices of its portfolio to each high-growth stock. The QQQ also doesn't include most of the S&P 500's slower-growth blue chip stocks.

Since QQQ is passively managed, it charges only a 0.18% expense ratio. That's much lower than the average expense ratio of 0.44% for actively managed ETFs.

Why will QQQ keep growing?

QQQ's top holdings are all exposed to the secular expansion of the cloud and AI markets. Those tailwinds won't dissipate anytime soon.

According to Grand View Research, the cloud computing and AI markets could grow at CAGRs of 16% and 30.6%, respectively, from 2026 to 2033. If you want to capitalize on those trends but don't have the time to research individual AI chipmakers, cloud infrastructure providers, and AI software makers, it's a good idea to simply buy a basket of the top 100 companies.

Past performance never guarantees future gains, but QQQ has delivered an impressive total return of 549% over the past ten years, beating the S&P 500's total return of 324%. So if you can withstand some near-term volatility and don't plan to withdraw your money from the market for at least a few more years, it's a great idea to accumulate QQQ if the market crashes.
